# Local resolution weighting

Local resolution weighting (LRW) combines acquisitions so that each pixel comes
mostly from the acquisitions with the highest spatial resolution there. The method was
introduced by Small et al. (2022)[^small] and is how s1bursts composes RTC
backscatter and coherence.

## Why mountains need it

A radar sees mountain slopes very unevenly. A slope facing the satellite is
squeezed into a few pixels, so its detail is coarse. A slope facing away is
stretched over many pixels and seen in fine detail, unless it is so steep that
it falls into shadow. Which slopes are seen well depends on the direction the
satellite looks from, so different orbits complement each other.

## How the weights work

The weight of each acquisition comes from its `scattering_area` band. This band
gives, for every pixel, the area of ground that the radar mixed into it,
relative to a reference: large on slopes facing the satellite, small on slopes
facing away. Its inverse is the local resolution, and LRW uses it as the
weight:

$$
W_i = \frac{1/A_i}{\sum_j 1/A_j}, \qquad
\text{composite} = \sum_i W_i \, \gamma^0_i
$$

Here $A_i$ is the scattering area of acquisition $i$ and $\gamma^0_i$ its
backscatter. An acquisition that sees a pixel twice as finely counts twice as
much there. A pixel without a valid area, such as one in shadow, gets no
weight.

Bursts from the same orbit and date are joined first, so the overlap between
neighboring bursts is not counted twice.

## The quality layers

Two quality layers describe each composite. `QA-NUM` counts the acquisitions
that contributed to each pixel. `QA-CQM`, the composite quality map, rates the
combined resolution:

$$
\text{CQM} = \frac{1}{\sum_i W_i A_i}
$$

A higher CQM means finer combined detail. CQM describes viewing geometry only;
it is not an uncertainty and says nothing about how accurate the backscatter
is. With `aggregation="median"` or a quantile, CQM is still computed from the
weighted mean of the areas, so it describes the weighting rather than the
particular acquisitions that supplied each value.

## Limiting extreme weights

A slope facing almost directly away from the satellite can get a very small
area and therefore a very large weight. `clip_max_resolution` caps the weight
to keep one acquisition from dominating such pixels. Report the cap if you use
it.

[^small]: Small, D., Rohner, C., Miranda, N., Ruetschi, M., & Schaepman, M. E.
    (2022). Wide-area analysis-ready radar backscatter composites. *IEEE
    Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*, 60, 5201814.
    <https://doi.org/10.1109/TGRS.2021.3055562>
